a: The teaching of the Lord
p: The manuscript gives the book a short title and a long one. This line is the long one.
b: Lake prints two titles above chapter 1. The short one, ΔΙΔΑΧΗ ΤΩΝ ΔΩΔΕΚΑ ΑΠΟΣΤΟΛΩΝ (Didachē tōn dōdeka apostolōn), which the digital text leaves out but Lake's printed page has, "Teaching of the Twelve Apostles," is the name the book goes by. The long one, translated here, says whose teaching it claims to be (the Lord's), who handed it on (the Twelve) and who it is for (the Gentiles). Didachē means "teaching" or "instruction," the word Acts 2:42 uses for "the teaching of the apostles." No apostle is named as writer, and the book never says who wrote it. Eusebius knew a book he called "the so-called Teachings of the Apostles" and counted it among the "rejected writings" (Church History 3.25.4, in McGiffert's translation; Kraft gives Eusebius's Greek word as notha, "illegitimate").

a: the twelve apostles
p: The title ties the book to the Twelve, but the text never claims an apostle wrote it.
b: The title presents the book as the Lord's teaching passed on by the Twelve. That is a claim about where the teaching comes from, like Matthew 28:20 ("teaching them to keep everything I have commanded you"), not a signature. Inside the book, "apostles" are traveling teachers whom the church tests and sends on after a day or two (11:3-6); Lake notes that there the word "does not mean a member of 'the Twelve'" but an inspired teacher who preaches, "very much what is now called a Missionary." Kraft thinks the editor's "whole aim seems to be to let the 'apostolic' teachings speak for themselves." Lake thought the book composite: an older Two Ways, an early church manual, and a recension in this manuscript that "can scarcely be later than the second century."

a: to the Gentiles
p: Tois ethnesin: the teaching is addressed to non-Jews who are turning to God.
b: Ethnē is "the nations," and where it means non-Jews as people the site says "the Gentiles," as in Paul and Acts. The title marks the book as instruction for Gentile converts. Much of chapters 1-6 is moral teaching Jews already gave (the commandments of 2:2-3; the "my child" sayings of chapters 3-4), and Lake reports that "many think" the Two Ways was "a Jewish pre-Christian document, used for catechetical purposes, perhaps especially among Proselytes." The book also uses "the Gentiles" for outsiders (1:3), as Matthew 5:47 does.
orig: τοῖς ἔθνεσιν (tois ethnesin)

a: There are two ways
p: Life and death set before the hearer as two paths: an old picture from the Law and the Prophets.
b: Moses sets "life and what is good, death and what is bad" before Israel (Deuteronomy 30:15) and tells them, "Choose life" (Deuteronomy 30:19). Jeremiah gives the LORD's word: "Look, I am setting before you the way of life and the way of death" (Jeremiah 21:8). Psalm 1 contrasts the way of the righteous and the way of the wicked, and Jesus speaks of the cramped road "leading to life" (Matthew 7:14). The same teaching, with "the way of light" and "the way of darkness," closes the Epistle of Barnabas (Barnabas 18-20). Lake: the first part of the Didache "is always known as 'The Two Ways'."

a: a great difference between the two ways
p: Didache 1-6 and Barnabas 18-20 share one moral teaching. Who borrowed from whom is not settled.
b: The Two Ways of the Didache and the closing chapters of the Epistle of Barnabas share long runs of the same Greek. Lake saw three possibilities: Barnabas used the Didache, the Didache used Barnabas, or both used a common source. "The matter is not clear, but probably the majority of scholars incline to the last view, and many think that the common source ... was a Jewish pre-Christian document, used for catechetical purposes." Lake also lists a Latin version, "either of a part of our Didache, or of a cognate document," known from two copies, among the witnesses to the original Teaching. The Didache's form is longer and more orderly; Barnabas arranges the same sayings loosely and under light and darkness.

a: you are to love the God who made you
p: The way of life opens with Jesus' two commandments, with God named as Maker.
b: Jesus answers the question about the great commandment with Deuteronomy 6:5 and Leviticus 19:18: "Love the Lord your God with all your heart" (Matthew 22:37) and "A second one is like it: 'You are to love your neighbor as yourself'" (Matthew 22:39). The Didache keeps "first" and "second," as Matthew and Mark do (Mark 12:29-31), but names God as "the God who made you," the Creator whom Gentile converts were turning to. The phrase returns at 5:2, where the people on the way of death "do not know the one who made them."

a: whatever you would not want to happen to you
t: The Golden Rule, said the other way
p: The Didache gives the rule in its negative form: do not do what you would not want done to you.
b: Jesus gives the rule positively: "So then, whatever you want people to do for you, do the same for them" (Matthew 7:12; compare Luke 6:31). The Didache has the negative form, which was common in Jewish teaching: Tobit 4:15 has a negative form too. Codex Bezae adds the negative rule to the apostles' decree for the Gentiles in Acts 15:20 and 15:29 (see the variants there). The two forms say the same thing from two sides; the Didache's goes with its long list of "You must not" commands in chapter 2.

a: The teaching of these words is this
p: 1:3-2:1 is a block of Jesus' sayings that Barnabas's Two Ways does not have.
b: After the two commandments, the Didache explains them with sayings like those of the Sermon on the Mount and Luke's Sermon on the Plain (1:3-1:6), then picks up again with "The teaching's second commandment" (2:1). Barnabas 18-20 has nothing like this block, nor does the Latin Two Ways, and Kraft thinks it "most probable" that it was put into the Two Ways at one of the latest stages, "a Christian contribution that may have been added by the Didachist himself." Lake's footnote at 1:5 (that the passage on giving is also in Hermas, "and suggests that this part of the Didache is later than Hermas (c. 140 A.D.)") points the same way. Two other witnesses touch this block: the Greek papyrus from Oxyrhynchus (P.Oxy. 1782, late fourth century) has 1:3b-4a "in a slightly variant form," with a longer 1:4a, and the Georgian version lacks 1:5-6 altogether (Kraft).

a: Bless the ones who curse you
p: The words follow Luke 6:28, then Matthew's "pray for ... the people who persecute you," with fasting added.
b: "Bless the ones who curse you" is Luke 6:28 in the Byzantine text, with hymin ("to you"); the SBLGNT has hymas. "Pray for your enemies" joins Matthew 5:44 ("keep loving your enemies, and pray for the people who persecute you"), and then the Didache adds something no Gospel says: "fast for the people who persecute you." "What thanks is there" (poia charis) is Luke's word (Luke 6:32), and "Don't even the Gentiles do the same?" is Matthew's (Matthew 5:47). The closing promise, "and you will have no enemy," is the Didache's own. Kraft thinks the Didache "probably" does not depend directly on the written Gospels but used material "which continued to circulate (in various forms) after they were written," following H. Koester.
orig: εὐλογεῖτε τοὺς καταρωμένους ὑμῖν (eulogeite tous katarōmenous hymin)

a: the desires of flesh and body
p: The opening echoes 1 Peter 2:11, "keep away from the flesh's desires."
b: "Keep away from the flesh's desires" (1 Peter 2:11) is nearly the same Greek (apechesthai tōn sarkikōn epithymiōn); the Didache adds "and bodily." It stands oddly between the sayings on enemies and the sayings on the other cheek, and Lake's margin points to 1 Peter and to Titus 2:12. Here "desires" (epithymiai) are the cravings of the body in general; in 3:3 the same word leads "to sexual sin."
orig: ἀπέχου τῶν σαρκικῶν καὶ σωματικῶν ἐπιθυμιῶν (apechou tōn sarkikōn kai sōmatikōn epithymiōn)

a: and you will be perfect
p: Matthew ends the same sayings with "you are to be perfect" (5:48). The Didache uses the word again at 6:2.
b: "So you are to be perfect, the way your heavenly Father is perfect" (Matthew 5:48) closes the sayings on enemies; the Didache places "you will be perfect" after turning the other cheek. Teleios means complete, full-grown, whole. The word returns at 6:2: whoever can carry "the whole yoke of the Lord" "will be perfect," and whoever cannot is to do what he can. The Didache does not treat perfection as an extra for a few; it is the goal of the teaching, and 10:5 and 16:2 pray that the church be "made perfect" at the end.
orig: τέλειος (teleios)

a: drafts you into service for one mile
p: Angareuō: soldiers and officials could make a local man carry baggage for a set distance.
b: The verb is the one Matthew uses when soldiers force Simon of Cyrene to carry the cross (Matthew 27:32) and in the same saying (Matthew 5:41: "When someone drafts you into service for one mile, go with him for two"). The Didache's Greek here is Matthew's almost exactly. The point is the same in both: answer forced service with more than is forced.
orig: ἀγγαρεύσῃ (angareusē)

a: You could not, anyway
p: The short Greek oude gar dynasai is a puzzle. It may mean a Christian has no right to take it back.
b: Literally, "for you are not even able." Kraft calls the words obscure and gives three senses for the older tradition: not taking the man to court (1 Corinthians 6:1-7), resignation ("you are helpless to resist"), or giving without holding back. Lake's English, "not even if thou canst," makes it a concession: do not ask for it back, even if you could. The Plain English Translation keeps the bare words and leaves the reason open. Luke 6:30 has the command without any reason: "When someone carries off your things, do not ask for them back."
orig: οὐδὲ γὰρ δύνασαι (oude gar dynasai)

a: Keep giving to anyone who asks you
t: Giving without limit, then a limit
p: The command is Luke 6:30. The rest of the verse warns those who take without need.
b: "Keep giving to anyone who asks you" is Luke 6:30 (panti tō aitounti se didou, with the article as in the Byzantine text). The Didache then explains it: God wants his own gifts shared with all, the giver who obeys is "innocent," and the one who takes what he does not need will answer for it. The Shepherd of Hermas has the same teaching in its Commandment 2: "Give to all, for God wishes His gifts to be shared among all," and those who receive "will render an account to God why and for what they have received" (as translated at New Advent). Lake's footnote says the passage is "found in the 4th mandate of Hermas"; the text opened for this page has it in the second.

a: his own gracious gifts
p: Charismata: the same word Paul uses for the Spirit's gifts, here meaning everything God gives.
b: Ek tōn idiōn charismatōn, "from his own gracious gifts." The giver is only passing on what came from the Father, so he has no claim to hold it back. In Paul, charismata are mostly the gifts of the Spirit (1 Corinthians 12:4); here it is God's generosity in general, including money and food. "His own" could also mean the giver's own gifts; the sentence reads more easily of the Father, as Hermas also has it ("His gifts").
orig: ἐκ τῶν ἰδίων χαρισμάτων (ek tōn idiōn charismatōn)

a: until he has paid off the last cent
p: Jesus' words about debt and prison (Matthew 5:26) are turned toward people who take alms they do not need.
b: In Matthew the saying is about making peace with an opponent before court: "you will not come out of there until you have paid off the last cent" (Matthew 5:26). The Didache applies the words to someone who lives on gifts he does not need: he will be "put in custody" (en synochē, "in confinement" or "in distress") and questioned. Whether it means a human court, God's judgment, or both is not said.
orig: τὸν ἔσχατον κοδράντην (ton eschaton kodrantēn)

a: Let your alms sweat in your hands
t: A saying from no known book
p: "Let your alms sweat in your hands" is quoted as something "said," but no Bible book has it.
b: "It has been said" (eirētai) introduces a quotation, yet no book of the Bible has these words. The image is of a coin held so long in a closed fist that it grows damp: think before you give, and find out who should get it. That seems to pull against 1:5 ("Keep giving to anyone who asks you"), and the two may come from different layers of the book. Sirach has a similar idea: "If you do a kindness, know who you are doing it for" (Sirach 12:1). Whether the saying is meant as a word of the Lord, of Scripture, or of a wise teacher is not stated.

a: alms
p: Eleēmosynē, from the word for mercy: a gift to the poor.
b: Eleēmosynē comes from eleos, "mercy," and means a gift made out of pity for someone in need; English "alms" comes from it through Latin. It is the word in Matthew 6:2-4 ("whenever you give to the poor") and in Tobit's praise of giving (Tobit 12:9). The Didache returns to it at 15:4: "Your prayers, your alms and all your deeds."
orig: ἐλεημοσύνη (eleēmosynē)

a: The teaching's second commandment
p: The list of 2:2-7 is called the second commandment: loving your neighbor spelled out.
b: In 1:2 the way of life is first love of God, second love of neighbor. Chapter 2 opens "the second commandment" and lists what love of neighbor forbids, much as Paul says the commands "Do not commit adultery," "Do not murder," "Do not steal" "are all gathered up in this saying: 'You are to love your neighbor as yourself'" (Romans 13:9). Kraft notes that the block 1:3b-2:1 is missing from Barnabas and the Latin Two Ways, which suggests that an older form ran straight from 1:2 to 2:2.

a: You must not murder. You must not commit adultery.
p: The list starts with the second table of the Ten Commandments and adds sins of the Greek and Roman world.
b: The list keeps the order of Matthew 19:18 and Exodus 20:13-17 (murder, adultery, stealing, false testimony, craving), but after each of the old commands it adds sins that Gentile converts would meet around them: the abuse of boys after adultery; sexual sin; magic and potions; abortion and the killing of newborns. So it reads like the commandments applied to a pagan city. Each line uses the Greek future with ou, the form of the Ten Commandments in the Greek Old Testament, which the site renders "You must not."

a: sexually abuse boys
p: Paidophthoreō, "corrupt boys," names the Greek custom of men taking boys as sexual partners.
b: The verb joins pais ("boy, child") and phthoreō ("corrupt, ruin"). Kraft: the word "literally reads 'do not be a corrupter of children/boys'" and refers to men using boys sexually; he points to Philo among Jewish writers who discuss the practice at length, and notes that the word was later widened to same-sex acts in general, as the Apostolic Constitutions takes it here. Barnabas's Two Ways has the same line (Barnabas 19:4). The subject is the abuse of children, not the adult relations the site's topic on same-sex relations treats. Lake's English hides the sense; the Plain English Translation says what the word names. It stands right after adultery, among the sexual sins.
orig: παιδοφθορήσεις (paidophthorēseis)

a: make magic potions
p: Mageuō is to practice magic; pharmakeuō to make drugs and potions, for spells or for poison.
b: Pharmakon was any drug: medicine, poison, love potion or charm. The site's New Testament renders pharmakeia "sorcery" (Galatians 5:20) and pharmaka "magic potions" (Revelation 9:21). The verb here stands just before the line on abortion; the text does not say whether the two are linked. Mageuō, from the Persian magoi, is the word for Simon in Samaria, "practicing magic" (Acts 8:9).
orig: οὐ μαγεύσεις, οὐ φαρμακεύσεις (ou mageuseis, ou pharmakeuseis)

a: You must not murder a child by abortion
t: Abortion and the killing of newborns
p: "Murder a child en phthora," in destruction: abortion, and then the killing of newborns. Barnabas 19:5 has the same line.
b: Literally "murder a child in destruction" (phthora, ruin, destruction), "and do not kill one that has been born." Kraft: the first line refers to abortion, "apparently before birth since infanticide is next mentioned," and the Latin Two Ways has "abortion" here. The Didache calls the unborn a "child" (teknon) and the act "murder." Some Greeks accepted both acts: Aristotle proposed a law "that no deformed child shall be reared," and that a child conceived against the rules be aborted "before it has developed sensation and life" (Politics 7, 1335b, Rackham's translation). Josephus says the Law "forbids women to cause abortion of what is begotten" (Against Apion 2.202). Exodus 21:22-23 is read in more than one way, and its Greek translation sets a different law from the Hebrew (see the notes there). Barnabas 19:5 has the same line, and Didache 5:2 lists "murderers of children" on the way of death.
orig: οὐ φονεύσεις τέκνον ἐν φθορᾷ, οὐδὲ γεννηθὲν ἀποκτενεῖς (ou phoneuseis teknon en phthora, oude gennēthen apokteneis)

a: crave what belongs to your neighbor
p: "You must not crave" is the site's Exodus 20:17. The Didache shortens the list to "your neighbor's things."
b: Exodus 20:17 lists the neighbor's house, wife, slaves and animals, "or anything at all that belongs to your neighbor." The Didache keeps only the summary, ta tou plēsion, "the things of your neighbor." Its list then turns from deeds to words (2:3-5) and inner attitudes (2:6), the way Jesus takes the commands inward in Matthew 5.

a: You must not swear falsely
p: "You must not swear falsely" is the very wording of Matthew 5:33; false testimony is Matthew 19:18.
b: Ouk epiorkēseis is the old command Jesus quotes in Matthew 5:33 ("You must not swear falsely") before he says not to swear at all. "You must not give false testimony" is Matthew 19:18's form of the ninth commandment. The last two lines go beyond the commandments: no speaking badly of others, and no "remembering wrongs" (mnēsikakeō, to nurse an old injury), as in Leviticus 19:18, "do not keep a grudge against the children of your people," the verse that goes on, "You are to love your neighbor as yourself."
orig: οὐκ ἐπιορκήσεις ... οὐ μνησικακήσεις (ouk epiorkēseis ... ou mnēsikakēseis)

a: two-minded or two-tongued
p: Dignōmōn and diglōssos: saying one thing to one person and another to the next.
b: Dignōmōn is "of two opinions," changeable; diglōssos is "double-tongued," telling each listener what he wants to hear. 1 Timothy 3:8 says deacons "should not say one thing to one person and another to the next" (Greek dilogous). Sirach warns against the double-tongued in the same way (Sirach 5:9; 28:13). The Didache calls such speech "a death trap," literally "a snare of death"; Proverbs too speaks of "death's traps" (Proverbs 14:27).
orig: διγνώμων οὐδὲ δίγλωσσος (dignōmōn oude diglōssos)

a: filled with action
p: Your word must be "filled full with action," not left empty.
b: Memestōmenos praxei: a word stuffed full of doing. An empty (kenos) word is one with nothing behind it. Compare Jesus' warning that people "will have to answer" for "every idle word" (Matthew 12:36), and James on hearing and doing (James 1:22). Barnabas has no line like this one.
orig: μεμεστωμένος πράξει (memestōmenos praxei)

a: Some you are to correct, some you are to pray for
p: Three ways of treating people instead of hate: correct some, pray for some, love some more than yourself.
b: The verse widens "You must not hate anyone" into three duties. Correcting (elenchō) is a form of love, as in Leviticus 19:17 ("Be sure to correct your fellow citizen") and Matthew 18:15 ("go and correct him"). Praying covers those who cannot be corrected. "Love more than yourself" (literally "beyond your soul") goes beyond "as yourself" (1:2); Barnabas 19:5 also tells the reader to love the neighbor more than his own soul. The three groups could be outsiders, weaker believers and fellow believers, but the text does not say.

a: My child
p: The teacher speaks to a learner like a father to a son, as the wisdom books do.
b: "My son" is the voice of Proverbs (Proverbs 1:8; 2:1) and Sirach (Sirach 2:1), where a teacher passes on wisdom to a pupil. The Didache uses teknon mou six times in 3:1-4:1 and turns to the plural "children" at 5:2. The form suits teaching given to someone preparing for baptism (7:1: "First say all these things"). Barnabas uses "children" for his readers too.

a: every evil thing
t: Every evil, or every evil man?
p: Pantos ponērou can be "every evil thing" or "every evil person."
b: The Greek ending fits both. Lake reads it of people ("every evil man and from all like him"); the Plain English Translation reads it of things, because the verses that follow are about sins and what leads to them. Either way the call is the one in 1 Thessalonians 5:22, to keep away from every kind of evil, and to run from what is "like it," the small sins that lead to large ones.
orig: ἀπὸ παντὸς πονηροῦ (apo pantos ponērou)

a: anger leads the way to murder
p: 3:2-6 traces each great sin back to a small one: anger to murder, desire to adultery, lying to theft.
b: Each saying has the same shape: do not be X, for X "leads the way to" a great sin; do not be Y or Z either, "for from all these things" that sin "is born." The pattern is like Jesus' teaching that anger is already liable to judgment and lustful looking already adultery (Matthew 5:21-22, 27-28). Jewish teachers spoke of building "a fence around the Torah," keeping far from the line so as not to cross it, and these verses work the same way. The five great sins are murder, adultery, idol worship, theft and blasphemy.

a: have a roving eye
p: Hypsēlophthalmos, "lifting the eyes high": here, letting the eyes rove after women.
b: The rare word means "high-eyed." Elsewhere lifted eyes can mean pride, but here it stands among the roots of adultery, so it means eyes that wander and stare. Jesus says that looking at a woman to desire her is already adultery in the heart (Matthew 5:28), and Job made a covenant with his eyes (Job 31:1). "Foul in speech" (aischrologos) is the vice of Colossians 3:8, "foul words out of your mouth."
orig: ὑψηλόφθαλμος (hypsēlophthalmos)

a: do not read omens from birds
p: Four kinds of fortune-telling and magic: birds, spells, stars and magical cleansing.
b: An oiōnoskopos read signs from birds (Kraft: "augury (literally, interpreting behavior of birds)"). An epaoidos chanted spells; a mathēmatikos (literally "one who studies," the word for astrologers) read the stars; and a perikathairōn did rites of magical purifying. The Law forbade Israel all such things (Deuteronomy 18:10-12). The Didache adds "do not even want to look at these things": to watch them out of curiosity is the first step on the road to idol worship.
orig: οἰωνοσκόπος ... ἐπαοιδὸς ... μαθηματικὸς ... περικαθαίρων (oiōnoskopos ... epaoidos ... mathēmatikos ... perikathairōn)

a: lying leads the way to stealing
p: The link between lying and stealing is not explained; the next words, love of money and empty glory, suggest why.
b: A liar finds it easy to cheat, and cheating is theft, so the step from one to the other is short. The verse adds two more roots: being "fond of money" (philargyros, the word for the Pharisees in Luke 16:14 and for the people of the last days in 2 Timothy 3:2) and being "hungry for empty glory" (kenodoxos, as in Galatians 5:26). Both make a person want more than is his.
orig: φιλάργυρος μηδὲ κενόδοξος (philargyros mēde kenodoxos)

a: complaining leads the way to blasphemy
p: Israel's grumbling in the wilderness ended in words against God.
b: Gongysos is a grumbler, the word Jude uses for people "who complain about their lot in life" (Jude 1:16). In the wilderness Israel's complaining turned into speaking against God (Numbers 14:2-11; 21:5), and Paul warns, "do not grumble, as some of them grumbled" (1 Corinthians 10:10). Here blasphēmia is speech that insults God; the same word can mean slander of people, but the setting (grumbling against one's lot) points to God.
orig: γόγγυσος (gongysos)

a: the gentle will inherit the earth
p: The words are nearly Matthew 5:5 in Greek, without "Blessed," and Psalm 37:11 lies behind both.
b: Hoi praeis klēronomēsousi tēn gēn is nearly Matthew 5:5, "Blessed are the gentle, because they will inherit the earth," but without "Blessed," and with "since" (epei) where Matthew has "because they" (hoti autoi). Matthew in turn takes it from Psalm 37:11, where the Hebrew says "the humble will take possession of the land." The Didache does not say it is quoting; the saying had become part of Christian teaching. "Gentle" (praus) is the quality Jesus claims in Matthew 11:29, and the Didache asks it of overseers and deacons too (15:1).
orig: οἱ πραεῖς κληρονομήσουσι τὴν γῆν (hoi praeis klēronomēsousi tēn gēn)

a: Tremble at all times at the words you have heard
p: An echo of Isaiah 66:2, the one God looks to is the one "who trembles at my word."
b: "The poor one, stricken in spirit, who trembles at my word" (Isaiah 66:2) is the person God looks on with favor. The words "you have heard" are the teaching being given now; the learner hears them before baptism (7:1). Barnabas 19:4 has nearly the same line. The virtues before it (slow to anger, merciful, free of evil, quiet, good) are the opposites of the vices of 3:2-6.

a: the high and mighty
p: Do not cling to the lofty; live among the righteous and the lowly. Paul says nearly the same.
b: "Do not set your minds on lofty things, but go along with the lowly" (Romans 12:16). The Didache's hypsēloi, "lofty ones," are the proud and powerful, and the soul "sticking" to them (kollaomai, "be glued to") pictures a person who attaches himself to them for advantage. Its opening line recalls Jesus' warning: "everyone who raises himself up will be brought low" (Luke 14:11).
orig: μετὰ ὑψηλῶν (meta hypsēlōn)

a: without God nothing happens
p: Accept whatever happens as good, since nothing happens apart from God.
b: The sentence teaches trust in God's providence, as in Jesus' saying that not one sparrow falls to the ground "without your Father" (Matthew 10:29) and Paul's "all things work together toward good for those who love God" (Romans 8:28). It does not say that evil events are good in themselves; the Greek energēmata means "workings, happenings," and the learner is to receive them "as good," in trust. Barnabas 19:6 has the same line.
orig: ἄτερ θεοῦ οὐδὲν γίνεται (ater theou ouden ginetai)

a: honor him as the Lord
p: Whoever speaks God's word is to be honored "as the Lord," because the Lord is present where his lordship is spoken of.
b: Hōs kyrion may mean "as the Lord" or "as a lord, a master." The reason given points to the first: "where the Lord's lordship (kyriotēs) is spoken of, the Lord is there." That is close to Jesus' words, "Whoever takes you in takes me in" (Matthew 10:40), and to Matthew 18:20, where two or three gathered in his name have him "right there in the middle of them." The same "as the Lord" returns for teachers and apostles at 11:2 and 11:4. Barnabas 19:9-10 has a related line: love the one who speaks the Lord's word to you "as the apple of your eye" and remember the day of judgment night and day.
orig: τιμήσεις δὲ αὐτὸν ὡς κύριον (timēseis de auton hōs kyrion)

a: the faces of the saints
p: Hoi hagioi, "the holy ones": here, the believers. The learner is to seek their company daily.
b: "The saints" are God's holy people, the members of the church, as in Paul's greetings ("to all the saints in Christ Jesus who live in Philippi," Philippians 1:1). "Seek out the faces" is a Hebrew way of saying "seek the presence, the company." The learner who is preparing for baptism is to spend time with believers every day and "find rest in their words," as the first believers in Acts met day after day (Acts 2:46). The word returns at 10:6 ("Whoever is holy, let him come") and 16:7.
orig: τὰ πρόσωπα τῶν ἁγίων (ta prosōpa tōn hagiōn)

a: long for a split
p: The manuscript says "You must not long for a split." Many editors change one letter to "make a split."
b: Lake prints pothēseis, "long for, desire," the manuscript's word, and notes that "the editors usually emend to poiēseis 'make'." Barnabas 19:12 has ou poiēseis schisma, with "make," which is why editors change the Didache. The Plain English Translation follows Lake and the manuscript; see the variant. "Split" (schisma) is the word Paul uses for the divisions at Corinth (1 Corinthians 1:10) and in Galatians 5:20 ("splits").
orig: οὐ ποθήσεις σχίσμα (ou pothēseis schisma)

a: you must not play favorites
p: "Taking a face" is the Bible's idiom for favoritism, from Leviticus 19:15 and Deuteronomy 1:17.
b: Lambanein prosōpon, "to take a face," translates the Hebrew idiom for judging by who someone is. Moses told Israel's judges, "Do not play favorites when you judge" (Deuteronomy 1:17), and Leviticus 19:15 forbids honoring either the poor or the great in court. Paul says of God, "For with God there are no favorites" (Romans 2:11). Here the rule covers correcting a fellow believer's wrongs: no softer treatment for a friend or a person of standing.
orig: οὐ λήψῃ πρόσωπον (ou lēpsē prosōpon)

a: double-minded about whether it will happen or not
p: The Greek does not say what "it" is: perhaps God's judgment, perhaps an answer to prayer.
b: Dipsychēseis is "be double-minded," the word of James 1:8 ("He is a double-minded man, never steady on any road he takes"), where it is about asking God in faith. Here the object is left open: "whether it will be or not." It could be God's judgment, the fulfilment of his promises, the answer to a prayer, or (in a judging context, after 4:3) one's own verdict. Barnabas 19:5 has the same words.
orig: οὐ διψυχήσεις (ou dipsychēseis)

a: holds out his hands to take
p: The picture is from Sirach 4:31: the hand stretched out to take and pulled in when it is time to give.
b: "Do not keep your hand stretched out for taking / and pulled in tight when it comes to paying back" (Sirach 4:31). The Didache's line is nearly the same image, applied to giving to others. Barnabas 19:9 has it word for word. Paul quotes a saying of the Lord: "Giving is more blessed than receiving" (Acts 20:35).

a: give it as ransom for your sins
p: Alms as a ransom for sins: a Jewish teaching the Didache keeps. Churches read such words differently.
b: Lytrōsis hamartiōn, "ransom (or redemption) of sins." The thought has deep Jewish roots: Daniel tells the king to "break with your sins by doing what is right, and with your wrongs by showing mercy to the poor" (Daniel 4:27); Tobit says "Alms rescue from death, and they cleanse away every sin" (Tobit 12:9); Sirach says "sins are atoned for by alms" (Sirach 3:30). 1 Peter 4:8 says "love lays a cover over a great number of sins." How churches read such words is set out in the site's cards at Proverbs 16 ("Do human kindness and good works atone for sin?") and Tobit 4 ("Does giving to the poor take away sin?").
orig: δώσεις λύτρωσιν ἁμαρτιῶν σου (dōseis lytrōsin hamartiōn sou)
r: Daniel 4:27; Tobit 12:9; Sirach 3:30; Proverbs 16:6; 1 Peter 4:8; Barnabas 19:10

a: have everything in common with your brother
p: Like the first church in Jerusalem, where no one called what he owned his own (Acts 4:32).
b: "Not one of them called anything he owned his own. Instead, all they had belonged to them in common" (Acts 4:32). The Didache gives the same rule as part of the way of life, with a reason: those who share "what never dies" (God's gifts of life and knowledge, 9:3; 10:2) should share what dies too. Paul argues the same way to the Gentile churches about the gift for Jerusalem (Romans 15:27). The line does not abolish property; it forbids treating it as one's own against a brother in need.

a: take your hand off your son or your daughter
p: Literally "do not lift your hand from": do not neglect your children's training.
b: The idiom means "do not hold back your hand," that is, do not leave your children untaught and undisciplined. Proverbs says the same about discipline (Proverbs 13:24; 22:6). The positive side follows: "from their youth you are to teach them to fear God." Barnabas 19:5 has nearly the same line (ou mē arēs for ouk areis, and "fear of God" without "the"). Paul's "Raise them instead in the Lord's discipline and warning" is the same duty (Ephesians 6:4).
orig: οὐκ ἀρεῖς τὴν χεῖρά σου (ouk areis tēn cheira sou)

a: your slaves, men or women
t: Slaves and masters in one church
p: The Didache speaks to masters first: slaves who hope in the same God must not be ordered about in bitterness.
b: Doulos is a slave, and paidiskē a slave woman; the site says "slave" for doulos, because Greek and Roman slavery was ownership of a person, not hired service. The Didache does not call for an end to slavery, but it puts master and slave under "the God who is over both of you" and warns that a harsh master could drive a believing slave from fear of God. The reason given is God's calling: he does not choose "by their standing." Ephesians 6:9 tells masters to "stop the threats," since "with him there is no favoritism." Barnabas 19:7 has the same lines.

a: as to a figure of God
p: Typos: slaves are to treat their masters as standing for God.
b: Typos (gloss: Greek typos, "type") is a stamp, image or pattern; the site renders it "figure," as Romans 5:14 ("Adam is a figure of the one who was coming"). The master is not God, but slaves are to serve as if they served God through him, as Paul writes, "Slaves, obey your human masters with fear and trembling and a single-minded heart, as you would obey Christ" (Ephesians 6:5). "With modesty" is en aischynē, literally "in shame," here the sense of shame that keeps one from acting shamefully. Barnabas 19:7 has the same words.
orig: ὡς τύπῳ θεοῦ (hōs typō theou)

a: without adding or taking away anything
p: The rule Moses gave for God's commands (Deuteronomy 4:2) is applied to the teaching the learner received.
b: "Do not add anything to the word I am commanding you, and do not take anything away from it" (Deuteronomy 4:2; also Deuteronomy 12:32). Revelation ends with a similar warning about its own words (Revelation 22:18-19). "What you received" (ha parelabes) uses the verb for receiving a handed-on teaching, as in 1 Corinthians 15:3 ("what I also received"). Barnabas 19:11 has the same line.
orig: φυλάξεις δὲ ἃ παρέλαβες (phylaxeis de ha parelabes)

a: In the church you are to confess your wrongs
p: Confessing sins in the gathered church, before prayer.
b: En ekklēsia is "in the church," that is, in the gathered assembly, not in a building. The believer confesses his wrongs before praying, so as not to come to prayer "with a bad conscience." James 5:16 says, "confess your sins to each other," and 14:1 repeats the rule before the Sunday meal. The Didache does not say to whom the confession is made or how. Churches differ on what such texts teach about confession: the site's card at Psalm 32 ("Must sins be confessed to a priest?") gives the views.
orig: ἐξομολογήσῃ τὰ παραπτώματά σου (exomologēsē ta paraptōmata sou)

a: the way of death
p: A list of 22 sins, close to the vice lists of Paul and of Jesus' words in Mark 7.
b: Vice lists were common in Jewish and Greek moral teaching, and the New Testament has several (Romans 1:29-31; Galatians 5:19-21; Mark 7:21-22). The Didache's list begins with the sins of the commandments (murders, adulteries, thefts, false testimonies) in nearly the order of Matthew 15:19 ("murders, adulteries, acts of sexual immorality, thefts, false testimony, slanders"), then adds the sins of the tongue and of pride. Where the New Testament has the same word, the site uses its New Testament rendering ("sorcery" as Galatians 5:20, "greed," "deceit"). Barnabas 20:1 has a shorter list in a different order.

a: destroyers of what God has formed
p: Phthoreis plasmatos theou: "ruiners of God's formed thing," next to "murderers of children."
b: Plasma is a thing shaped by hand, as a potter shapes clay; God "formed" the man from the dust in Genesis 2:7, and the psalmist says to God, "you wove me together in my mother's womb" (Psalm 139:13). Coming right after "murderers of children," the phrase points to abortion; Kraft notes that the Latin Two Ways reads here "destroyers of their children, abortionists." It matches the line in 2:2 ("murder a child by abortion," en phthora, from the same root as phthoreis). Barnabas 20:2 has the same two phrases.
orig: φονεῖς τέκνων, φθορεῖς πλάσματος θεοῦ (phoneis teknōn, phthoreis plasmatos theou)

a: they do not wear themselves out for the one who is worn down
p: Ou ponountes epi kataponoumenō: they take no pains for the one ground down by pain.
b: The Greek plays on poneō ("toil, take pains") and kataponeō ("wear down, oppress"). The Plain English Translation keeps the play with "wear themselves out" and "worn down." The same verb returns a few words later: they "wear down the one who is in trouble." The sins in the second half of the verse are against the poor and the needy, the people the prophets defend (Isaiah 1:23; Amos 2:6-7).
orig: οὐ πονοῦντες ἐπὶ καταπονουμένῳ (ou ponountes epi kataponoumenō)

a: Children, may you be rescued from all these!
t: A prayer to end the way of death
p: The list ends in a prayer for the learners, with the verb of the Lord's Prayer's "rescue us."
b: Rhystheiēte is a wish: "may you be rescued." It is the verb of the Lord's Prayer in 8:2 ("rescue us from the evil one") and of the prayer for the church in 10:5. The teacher, who said "my child" in chapters 3-4, now speaks to "children," all the learners together.
orig: ῥυσθείητε, τέκνα (rhystheiēte, tekna)

a: leads you away from this way of the teaching
p: A warning against teachers who lead learners away: the theme of 11:1-2 and 16:3.
b: Planaō is "lead astray, make wander," the verb of Jesus' warning, "Be on your guard, so that no one leads you astray" (Matthew 24:4). Anyone who teaches otherwise "teaches you apart from God." The same test appears at 11:1-2: welcome the teacher who teaches these things, but not one who "teaches a different teaching, to do away with this one."
orig: μή τίς σε πλανήσῃ (mē tis se planēsē)

a: the whole yoke of the Lord
t: "The whole yoke" and "do what you can"
p: The Didache sets a full standard and makes room for those who cannot yet reach it.
b: A "yoke" was a common Jewish picture for the Law and its commands. Jesus says, "Lift my yoke onto yourselves ... For my yoke is kind to wear, and the load I give is light" (Matthew 11:29-30), and Peter at the council speaks of a yoke "that neither our ancestors nor we ourselves had the strength to carry" (Acts 15:10). "The whole yoke of the Lord" can mean (1) all of Jesus' teaching in chapters 1-5, with "perfect" as in 1:4 and Matthew 5:48; or (2) the Jewish Law, which Gentiles are encouraged but not required to keep in full, as 6:3 then speaks of food. Kraft reads 6:2 as an ideal "adapted to a more realistic position: 'do the best you can.'" Either way the book does not make full perfection the price of entry.
orig: ὅλον τὸν ζυγὸν τοῦ κυρίου (holon ton zygon tou kyriou)

a: food sacrificed to idols
t: The one food rule that is firm
p: "Carry what you can" about food, but no idol food. The rule matches the apostles' decree in Acts 15.
b: The apostles' letter told Gentile believers to "keep away from food sacrificed to idols" (Acts 15:29), and Paul discussed the question at length (1 Corinthians 8:1-13; 10:19-30), allowing market meat (1 Corinthians 10:25). The Didache is strict: "be very careful," for it is "the worship of dead gods." Kraft: it "drew the line at meat that had been slaughtered in pagan temples," in agreement with much of early Christianity (Acts 15:20; Revelation 2:14, 20), and he thinks 6:3 once listed the food laws Christians had taken over for Gentiles. Other food laws are left to what each person "can carry," which may mean the Jewish food laws or fasting from certain foods.
orig: ἀπὸ δὲ τοῦ εἰδωλοθύτου (apo de tou eidōlothytou)

a: the worship of dead gods
p: The idols are "dead": a Jewish taunt against idols that the church took over.
b: The Psalms mock idols that have mouths and cannot speak (Psalm 115:4-8), and the Wisdom of Solomon says, "But miserable are those who set their hopes on dead things" (Wisdom of Solomon 13:10). Paul reminds the Thessalonians how they "turned away from idols to God, to serve a God who lives and is true" (1 Thessalonians 1:9). "Worship" here is latreia, the word for religious service.
orig: λατρεία ... θεῶν νεκρῶν (latreia ... theōn nekrōn)
r: Psalm 115:4-8; 1 Thessalonians 1:9; 1 Corinthians 10:20; Wisdom of Solomon 13:10

a: First say all these things
p: Baptism comes after the Two Ways has been taught: a time of teaching comes first.
b: Tauta panta proeipontes, "having said all these things first," ties chapters 1-6 to baptism: the learner hears the way of life and the way of death, then is baptized. Lake describes the Two Ways as "a statement of the principles of Christian conduct, which is to be taught to catechumens before their baptism." In Acts, baptism often follows preaching at once (Acts 2:41; 8:36-38); here a period of teaching and fasting (7:4) comes first. Later churches made this the catechumenate, the time of preparing for baptism.
orig: ταῦτα πάντα προειπόντες (tauta panta proeipontes)

a: into the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit
p: The words are those of Matthew 28:19, given here as the words to say in baptism.
b: "Baptizing them into the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit" (Matthew 28:19): the Didache's Greek here is Matthew's exactly. In Acts, people are baptized "in the name of Jesus Christ" (Acts 2:38) or "into the name of the Lord Jesus" (Acts 19:5; compare Acts 8:16), and 9:5 below also speaks of those "baptized into the Lord's name." Kraft: the threefold formula is used here "rather than the also popular baptism 'in the name of Jesus'," but that "does not, however, necessarily imply a conscious, full-blown 'trinitarian' theology as it was later defined." The site's card at Matthew 28 asks whether the threefold words must be used.
orig: εἰς τὸ ὄνομα τοῦ πατρὸς καὶ τοῦ υἱοῦ καὶ τοῦ ἁγίου πνεύματος (eis to onoma tou patros kai tou huiou kai tou hagiou pneumatos)

a: in living water
p: Hydōr zōn, "living water," is running water from a spring or a stream, not still water.
b: In Greek and Hebrew, "living water" is water that flows, as against water standing in a cistern or a pool. The Law asked for it in some washings (Leviticus 14:5; 15:13, where the Hebrew is mayim chayyim). Jesus plays on the double sense when he offers the Samaritan woman "living water" (John 4:10). The Didache's order of preference is running water, then other water, then cold before warm, then pouring if there is not enough for any of these (7:2-3).
orig: ἐν ὕδατι ζῶντι (en hydati zōnti)

a: pour water three times onto the head
p: Pouring is allowed when there is not enough water. Kraft calls it "probably the earliest reference to that practice."
b: The Didache prefers baptism "in" water; Kraft takes 7:2-3 to mean that "immersion in a river or a spring (cold, flowing water) was preferred practice," with still water next, and pouring three times on the head "as a last resort," which is "probably the earliest reference to that practice in Christianity." Three pourings match the three names. The verse can be read as early permission for pouring, or as a fallback that shows immersion was the rule. The site's card at Acts 8 ("Must baptism be by immersion?") sets out the traditions; this page does not repeat it.
orig: ἔκχεον εἰς τὴν κεφαλὴν τρὶς ὕδωρ (ekcheon eis tēn kephalēn tris hydōr)

a: into the name of Father and Son and Holy Spirit
p: Here the Greek drops "the" before each name, unlike 7:1.
b: 7:1 has tou patros kai tou huiou kai tou hagiou pneumatos, with "the" before each name, as in Matthew 28:19; 7:3 has patros kai huiou kai hagiou pneumatos, without it. The Plain English Translation shows the difference by leaving out "the." The meaning is the same; the shorter form reads like a fixed formula.
orig: εἰς ὄνομα πατρὸς καὶ υἱοῦ καὶ ἁγίου πνεύματος (eis onoma patros kai huiou kai hagiou pneumatos)

a: the one being baptized should fast first
p: The one baptizing, the one baptized and others fast first; the candidate one or two days.
b: Fasting goes with prayer and with new beginnings in Acts: the church at Antioch fasted before sending Barnabas and Saul (Acts 13:2-3), and Saul himself went three days without food before Ananias baptized him (Acts 9:9, 18). In the Apostolic Constitutions, which rewrites the Didache, the candidate is likewise to fast before baptism (book 7, chapter 22). "You are to order" is literally "you order" (keleueis), a present tense used as a command, and shows the book speaking to the one in charge.
orig: προνηστευσάτω (pronēsteusatō)

a: the hypocrites
p: Kraft reads "the hypocrites" as Pharisees or practicing Jews. The words would also fit Christians who kept the same days.
b: "Hypocrite" (hypokritēs) first meant a stage actor. In Matthew 6 Jesus warns against praying, giving and fasting "like the hypocrites" (Matthew 6:2, 5, 16), and Matthew 23 aims the word at scribes and Pharisees. The Didache borrows the word and the setting. Kraft thinks the saying "originally may have referred to Pharisaic practices (cf. Matt. 23:13), although the Didachist might mean simply practicing Jews." The words would also fit Christians who still kept those days. Either way the church still fasts twice a week, but by design on other days. The site's topic anti-judaism traces how such words were later used against Jews.
orig: μετὰ τῶν ὑποκριτῶν (meta tōn hypokritōn)

a: on the second day of the week and the fifth
t: Monday and Thursday, Wednesday and Friday
p: The Didache moves the church's two weekly fasts away from Monday and Thursday, to Wednesday and Friday.
b: The days are counted from the Sabbath: deutera sabbatōn, "the second (day) of the week," is Monday; the fifth is Thursday; the fourth, Wednesday; and paraskeuē, "Preparation Day," the day before the Sabbath, Friday (Mark 15:42; John 19:31). The Pharisee in Jesus' parable says "Twice a week I fast" (Luke 18:12) but names no days. The Mishnah puts the first series of public fasts for rain on "a Monday, Thursday, and the following Monday" (Mishnah Taanit 2:9); that passage is about fasts in a drought, not a weekly custom. Kraft takes the Didache's Monday and Thursday as the "(Pharisaic) Jewish fasts," citing the Babylonian Talmud (Shabbat 24a), and notes that Wednesday and Friday fasts "were widely observed in early Christianity" (Tertullian; Clement of Alexandria). The Apostolic Constitutions keeps the rule, fasting "on the fourth day of the week, and on the day of the Preparation" (book 7, chapter 23, in the Ante-Nicene Fathers translation).

a: as the Lord commanded in his good news
p: Euangelion, the word behind "gospel": was it a written Gospel, or the message about Jesus?
b: The site renders euangelion "good news," the word behind "gospel." The Didache refers to it four times: here, and "as the decree of the good news says" (11:3), "the way you have it in the good news" (15:3), "in our Lord's good news" (15:4). The Lord's Prayer that follows is very close to Matthew's form, and 15:3-4 sound like pointing to a text, which fits a written Gospel, probably Matthew. Kraft takes the other view for 15:3-4: "Probably 'the gospel' here does not consciously refer to a written document accessible to all, but to the teachings of Jesus ... which were regularly repeated in community gatherings."
orig: ἐν τῷ εὐαγγελίῳ αὐτοῦ (en tō euangeliō autou)

a: Our Father, who is in heaven
p: The Didache's prayer is Matthew's, with four small differences and a closing line of praise.
b:
The Plain English Translation uses the site's Matthew 6:9-13 word for word except where the Greek differs:
"in heaven": Didache en tō ouranō (singular); Matthew en tois ouranois (plural). The English is the same.
"the debt": Didache tēn opheilēn (one debt); Matthew ta opheilēmata ("the debts").
"forgive": Didache aphiemen (present, "we forgive"), as in Codex Bezae and the Byzantine text of Matthew; the oldest Matthew manuscripts have aphēkamen ("have forgiven").
The ending: Didache hoti sou estin hē dynamis kai hē doxa eis tous aiōnas, "For yours is the power and the glory forever," with no "kingdom" and no "Amen."
See the variants at Matthew 6:12 and 6:13, and Luke's shorter prayer (Luke 11:2-4).

a: For yours is the power and the glory forever.
p: The Didache closes the Lord's Prayer with a two-part line of praise, without "kingdom" or "Amen."
b: The oldest manuscripts of Matthew end the prayer at "rescue us from the evil one," and the longer "For yours is the kingdom and the power and the glory forever. Amen" came in later (see the variant at Matthew 6:13). The Didache already has a two-part form, "the power and the glory," which suggests a line of praise was being added in worship. Kraft notes that this doxology "seems to have been known in Egypt (see the Coptic versions of Matt. 6:13) and Syria." Compare David's praise in 1 Chronicles 29:11. The Didache's own meal prayers end with the same words (9:4; 10:5), so the doxology may be the church's usual response.

a: bread for the coming day
p: Epiousios is a rare word. The site's Matthew 6:11 renders it "for the coming day."
b: The Didache has the same rare adjective, ton epiousion, as Matthew 6:11 and Luke 11:3. Its meaning has been argued since the early church: "for the coming day," "needed for existence," or "daily." The Plain English Translation uses the site's Matthew wording, and the note there gives the readings. In the Didache the prayer is followed by the meal prayers of chapters 9-10, where bread is thanked for as "spiritual food" (10:3).
orig: τὸν ἄρτον ἡμῶν τὸν ἐπιούσιον (ton arton hēmōn ton epiousion)

a: three times a day
p: Three fixed times of prayer, as Daniel kept them and as the Jewish day of prayer did.
b: Daniel "knelt, prayed and gave thanks before his God" "three times a day" (Daniel 6:10); the psalmist prays "At evening, at morning, at midday" (Psalm 55:17). The Mishnah sets times for the morning, afternoon and evening prayers (Mishnah Berakhot 4:1). The Didache puts the Lord's Prayer in the place of those prayers, three times daily. In Acts, Peter and John go up to the temple "for the hour of prayer" and Peter prays "Around the sixth hour" (Acts 3:1; Acts 10:9). The Apostolic Constitutions keeps the rule (book 7, chapter 24).

a: the thanksgiving
t: "The thanksgiving": the Lord's Supper, a meal, or both?
p: Eucharistia means "thanksgiving." Whether chapters 9-10 describe the Lord's Supper is the main question about them.
b: The site does not write "Eucharist" here, because that would decide the question. The prayers of 9-10 thank God over a cup and broken bread, end with "after you have eaten your fill" (10:1), and say nothing of Jesus' body and blood or of his death. Kraft sets out the readings. (1) The Lord's Supper itself: "At first glance they seem to represent a 'Eucharist' liturgy"; 9:5 limits it to the baptized and calls it "what is holy." (2) A love feast: the meal in 10:1 and the separate rite of 14:1 "led many commentators to suggest" a fellowship meal like the "love feasts" of Jude 1:12; G. Dix (1945) took it so. (3) Kraft's own view: prayers from a love feast, used at a yearly service where the newly baptized shared their first Eucharist. The text also allows a full meal that was the Lord's Supper, as at Corinth (1 Corinthians 11:20-26). Lake's English says "Eucharist." See the chapter page.
orig: περὶ δὲ τῆς εὐχαριστίας (peri de tēs eucharistias)

a: First, about the cup
p: The cup comes first, then the bread, the reverse of the order in Paul and Mark.
b: In Mark 14:22-24 the bread comes first and then the cup; in 1 Corinthians 11:23-25 the cup comes "after the meal." The Didache thanks over the cup first. Lake's footnote: "this order 'first the Cup' is only found elsewhere in the earliest text of Lc. 22, 17 ff. (which omits v. 20) and perhaps in I. Cor. 10, 16." By "the earliest text" Lake probably meant the shorter text of Luke found in Codex Bezae and some Old Latin copies, since he says it "omits v. 20"; that text which has a cup before the bread and no cup after it; the site's Luke follows the longer text of nearly all manuscripts, which has both cups (see the variant at Luke 22:19). Paul names "the cup of blessing" before "the bread that we break" in 1 Corinthians 10:16. The Mishnah speaks of a blessing over wine drunk "before the meal" (Mishnah Berakhot 6:5).

a: the holy vine of your servant David
p: A rich image with no single meaning given: Israel as God's vine, the promise to David, or Jesus himself.
b: In the Psalms and prophets, Israel is the vine God planted ("A vine from Egypt you dug up and moved," Psalm 80:8; Isaiah 5:1-7). Jesus says "I am the real vine" (John 15:1), and in the Supper calls the wine "this produce of the vine" (Matthew 26:29). "The vine of David" may be the promise to David's house, the people of God gathered in David's son, or Jesus himself as David's heir. It is "made known" through Jesus, as "life and knowledge" are in 9:3. Over the cup, the Jewish blessing thanks God "Who creates fruit of the vine" (Mishnah Berakhot 6:1); the Didache's prayer thanks him for a different vine.

a: your servant David
p: Pais means both. The Didache calls David and Jesus pais of God in the same sentence.
b: Pais can be a child or a servant. The Greek Old Testament uses it for God's servant in Isaiah: "Look, my servant will succeed" (Isaiah 52:13), Greek ho pais mou, as in Isaiah 42:1. The early church's prayer in Acts uses it for both David and Jesus: "by the mouth of your servant David" (Acts 4:25) and "Jesus, your holy servant" (Acts 4:27). Since the Didache sets David and Jesus side by side with the same word, the site says "servant" in both, as in Acts; Lake has "child." The word returns in 9:3, 10:2 and 10:3.
orig: Δαυεὶδ τοῦ παιδός σου ... Ἰησοῦ τοῦ παιδός σου (Daueid tou paidos sou ... Iēsou tou paidos sou)
r: Acts 4:25; Acts 4:27; Acts 3:13; Isaiah 42:1; Isaiah 52:13; Matthew 12:18

a: the broken bread
p: Klasma is a broken piece; here the bread broken for sharing.
b: Klasma comes from klaō, "break," as in "break bread" (Acts 2:46; 20:7; Didache 14:1). In the feeding miracles the plural klasmata are the "broken pieces" left over (John 6:12). The Didache uses the singular for the bread on the table, so the site says "broken bread" in 9:3 and 9:4: the image of 9:4 is of grain scattered on the mountains and made into one loaf, not of scattered pieces put back together.
orig: περὶ δὲ τοῦ κλάσματος (peri de tou klasmatos)

a: life and knowledge
p: Gnōsis here is the knowledge of God made known through Jesus, not the secret knowledge of the later Gnostics.
b: The prayer thanks God for "life and knowledge" that he "made known" through Jesus, and 10:2 adds "knowledge and faith and immortality." Gnōsis later became the watchword of the Gnostic groups, who taught a hidden knowledge for a few. Nothing here is hidden: what is known is God himself, as in John 17:3 (eternal life is to know the only true God and Jesus Christ). The site always says "knowledge."
orig: ὑπὲρ τῆς ζωῆς καὶ γνώσεως (hyper tēs zōēs kai gnōseōs)

a: scattered over the mountains
p: The grain of one loaf grew on many mountains; the church, scattered over the earth, is to be gathered into one.
b: Orē are "mountains" or hill country. Bread is made from grain sown across many fields; once it is ground and baked, it is one loaf. Paul draws a similar lesson: "Because there is one loaf, we who are many are one body" (1 Corinthians 10:17). The prayer then asks for the gathering of the church "from the ends of the earth," the hope of Israel's prophets for the scattered tribes (Isaiah 11:12; Isaiah 43:5-6) and of Jesus' words about his chosen gathered "from the four winds" (Matthew 24:31; Didache 10:5). The Apostolic Constitutions keeps the picture: "as this grain was once scattered, and is now become one loaf" (book 7, in the Ante-Nicene Fathers translation), though, as Kraft notes, without the mountains; he adds that "many commentators" took the mountains as a sign of Syria or Palestine, where grain grew on hillsides, rather than Egypt.

a: For yours is the glory and the power through Jesus Christ forever.
p: The same closing praise as the Lord's Prayer (8:2), with the two words reversed and "through Jesus Christ" added.
b: In 8:2 the doxology is "For yours is the power and the glory forever." Here it is "the glory and the power," and the praise is given "through Jesus Christ," the only place in the meal prayers where the full name "Jesus Christ" appears. Paul likewise gives glory to God "through Jesus Christ" (Romans 16:27). The other short doxologies of chapters 9-10 ("To you be the glory forever") alternate with this longer form.

a: but only those baptized into the Lord's name
p: Only the baptized may eat and drink of the thanksgiving.
b: The rule ties the meal to baptism: those not yet baptized, including the learners of chapters 1-6, do not share it. The Lord's word quoted is Matthew 7:6 exactly, "Do not give what is holy to the dogs," which in Matthew has nothing to do with a meal; the Didache applies it to the thanksgiving. "Into the Lord's name" may be a short way of saying Christian baptism (compare 7:1). Kraft links the rule to the meal that followed baptism, "from which all nonbaptized persons were excluded." The Apostolic Constitutions keeps the rule: "Let no one eat of these things that is not initiated." Whether churches today should open or close the table is asked in the site's card at Matthew 7 ("Should communion be open to all who come?").

a: After you have eaten your fill
p: Meta to emplēsthēnai, "after being filled": the people have eaten a meal, not only a taste.
b: The verb is the one used of the crowds who "were filled" at the feeding of the five thousand (John 6:12, eneplēsthēsan). So the prayers of chapter 9 open a full meal and those of chapter 10 close it. This fits the Jewish order of blessings before and after a meal: the Mishnah describes the call to bless "the One from Whose food we have eaten" (Mishnah Berakhot 7:3) after eating. The Apostolic Constitutions changes this into "After the participation, give thanks in this manner," making it a prayer after communion.
orig: μετὰ δὲ τὸ ἐμπλησθῆναι (meta de to emplēsthēnai)

a: which you made to pitch its tent in our hearts
t: God's name living in his people
p: Kataskēnoō: God made his name "pitch its tent" in their hearts, as he once placed it in the Temple.
b: In Deuteronomy, God will choose a place "to make his name live there" (Deuteronomy 12:11), the sanctuary in Israel. The prayer moves that dwelling into the hearts of the believers. The verb is from skēnē, "tent," the word behind John 1:14: "the Word became flesh and pitched his tent among us." The thanksgiving then names what was made known through Jesus: knowledge, faith and immortality.
orig: οὗ κατεσκήνωσας ἐν ταῖς καρδίαις ἡμῶν (hou kateskēnōsas en tais kardiais hēmōn)

a: Master, the Almighty
p: Despota pantokrator: the God of the Jewish prayers, Lord of all creation.
b: Despotēs, "Master," is how the church addresses God in prayer in Acts 4:24, and pantokratōr, "the Almighty," is the Greek Old Testament's title for the LORD of Armies, used often in Revelation (Revelation 4:8). The prayer thanks God first for creation and for ordinary food and drink given to all people, then for "spiritual food and drink, and eternal life" given to the church. Lake's English says "eternal light," but his Greek has zōēn, "life." A fifth-century Coptic fragment begins in this verse and runs into 12:1-2; Kraft notes that it opens "... to the sons of man" and lacks "so that they might give you thanks."
orig: σύ, δέσποτα παντοκράτορ (sy, despota pantokrator)
r: Acts 4:24; Revelation 4:8; Revelation 4:11; Wisdom of Solomon 1:14

a: spiritual food and drink
p: The same words Paul uses of Israel's manna and water from the rock, which he links to the Supper.
b: "All of them ate the same spiritual food, and all of them drank the same spiritual drink" is how Paul describes Israel in the wilderness (1 Corinthians 10:3-4), just before he speaks of the cup and the bread (1 Corinthians 10:16). John 6 speaks of Jesus as the bread from heaven that gives eternal life (John 6:32-35, 54). The Didache sets ordinary food, given to all for enjoyment, beside the spiritual food given to the church "through your servant." The line fits a reading of these chapters as the Lord's Supper.

a: Gather it from the four winds
p: The prayer asks God to do what Jesus said his angels would do: gather the chosen from the four winds.
b: "He will send his angels out with a great trumpet, and they will gather together his chosen from the four winds" (Matthew 24:31). The prayer asks God to rescue his church "from every evil" (as the Lord's Prayer in 8:2), to make it "perfect" in his love (see 1:4; 16:2), and to gather it "into your kingdom that you prepared for it," as the King says to the righteous, "Receive what you inherit: the kingdom made ready for you" (Matthew 25:34). The church is "made holy" (hagiastheisa) by God, not by itself.
orig: σύναξον αὐτὴν ἀπὸ τῶν τεσσάρων ἀνέμων (synaxon autēn apo tōn tessarōn anemōn)

a: let this world pass away
p: The prayer longs for the end of this age and the coming of grace, as 1 Corinthians 7:31 and 1 John 2:17 speak.
b: "Let grace come" may mean the Lord himself, who brings grace (compare Titus 2:11, "God's grace has appeared"). "This world" (ho kosmos houtos) is the present order of things, of which John says, "The world is passing away" (1 John 2:17; compare 1 Corinthians 7:31). The cry looks forward to chapter 16 and fits "Marana tha" a few words later.
orig: ἐλθέτω χάρις καὶ παρελθέτω ὁ κόσμος οὗτος (elthetō charis kai parelthetō ho kosmos houtos)

a: Hosanna to the God of David!
p: The crowds in Matthew cry "Hosanna to the Son of David!" The witnesses of the Didache differ here.
b: "Hosanna to the Son of David!" is the crowd's cry as Jesus enters Jerusalem (Matthew 21:9), and the children's in the Temple (Matthew 21:15). Hōsanna comes from the Hebrew of Psalm 118:25 ("LORD, please, save us now!") and had become a shout of praise. The Greek manuscript has "the God of David." Kraft reports that the Coptic fragment has "house of David" and the Apostolic Constitutions "son of David" (book 7, chapter 26, in the Ante-Nicene Fathers translation: "Hosanna to the Son of David"), and he suggests the original may have been "to David's Lord" (Psalm 110:1), which "easily could give rise to the three preserved readings." See the variant.
orig: Ὡσαννὰ τῷ θεῷ Δαυείδ (Hōsanna tō theō Daueid)

a: Whoever is holy, let him come
p: An invitation and a warning: a call to the meal, or to the Lord who is coming.
b: The holy are called to "come," the unholy to repent. "Come" can be the call to pass from a meal to the Supper itself, or the call to the Lord's coming, joined to "Marana tha" and to "The Spirit and the bride say, 'Come!'" (Revelation 22:17). Kraft finds these lines "especially similar to Rev. 22:11, 20" and thinks 10:4-6 may be prayed in turn, a leader saying one line and the people the next. The Apostolic Constitutions turns it into "If any one be holy, let him draw near; but if any one be not such, let him become such by repentance."

a: Marana tha
p: Aramaic, "Our Lord, come!" Paul gives the same words to the Greek church at Corinth (1 Corinthians 16:22).
b: The Aramaic letters MRNTh' can be divided two ways: marana tha, "Our Lord, come!", or maran atha, "Our Lord has come" (or "is coming"). Lake prints maran atha; the site follows marana tha, as in its 1 Corinthians 16:22, because Revelation 22:20 gives the Greek of the prayer, "Come, Lord Jesus!" (see the variant). That Greek-speaking churches kept an Aramaic prayer shows it came from the first Aramaic-speaking believers, who called Jesus "Lord" and prayed for his coming. Here it closes the meal prayers, as Paul closes his letter with it.
orig: μαρὰν ἀθά (maran atha)

a: as much as they want
p: Prophets may give thanks "as much as they want": in their own words, or at greater length.
b: Hosa thelousin can mean "as long as they wish" or "in whatever words they wish." Either way, the written prayers are for the community, and prophets, who speak in the Spirit (11:7), are not bound to them. The Apostolic Constitutions gives this freedom to the presbyters instead of the prophets (book 7, chapter 26), a sign of how church leadership changed. After this verse the Coptic fragment and the Apostolic Constitutions add a thanksgiving over ointment, which the Greek manuscript and the Georgian version lack (Kraft).
orig: ὅσα θέλουσιν (hosa thelousin)

a: to do away with this one
t: Testing a teacher by his teaching
p: The test is the content: a teacher who undoes "all the things said above" is not to be heard.
b: The verb katalyō, "do away with, tear down," is the one Jesus uses: "I came not to do away with them but to fulfill them" (Matthew 5:17). A teacher who "adds righteousness and knowledge of the Lord" is welcomed "as the Lord" (compare 4:1). 2 John 1:10 gives a sharper rule: "If someone comes to you who does not bring this teaching, do not take him into the house."
orig: εἰς τὸ καταλῦσαι (eis to katalysai)

a: About the apostles and prophets
p: The Didache's "apostles" are not the Twelve but traveling preachers, Lake says: "what is now called a Missionary."
b: Lake: "'Apostle' in the Didache does not mean a member of 'the Twelve,' but is merely an inspired teacher who is engaged in preaching, especially to those as yet unconverted." The New Testament also uses "apostle" more widely than the Twelve: Barnabas (Acts 14:14), Andronicus and Junia (Romans 16:7), and the "false apostles" Paul fights at Corinth (2 Corinthians 11:13). Prophets travel too (Acts 11:27; 21:10). The Didache's rules (one or two days, no money, only bread for the road) are practical tests for a church that could not check a visitor's claims. Matthew 10:9-11 and Luke 10:4-7 give Jesus' own rules for his messengers.
r: Acts 14:14; Romans 16:7; 2 Corinthians 11:13; Acts 11:27; Matthew 10:9-11; Luke 10:4-7; 1 Corinthians 12:28

a: welcomed as the Lord
p: "Whoever takes you in takes me in" (Matthew 10:40): the messenger stands for the one who sent him.
b: The rule rests on Jesus' words to the Twelve: "Whoever takes you in takes me in, and whoever takes me in takes in the one who sent me" (Matthew 10:40). Hospitality to traveling believers was a duty (3 John 1:5-8; Hebrews 13:2), and also open to abuse, which is why the next verses set limits.

a: He is to stay only one day
t: One day, or not one day?
p: The manuscript lacks two little words, "except": Lake adds them from 12:2.
b: As the manuscript stands, the line reads "He will not stay one day," which makes no sense next to "and the next as well if there is need." Lake supplies ei mē, "except," and notes that "xii. 2 seems to make the correction quite certain," since 12:2 has the same phrase ("not ... except two or three days"). See the variant. An apostle who stays three days is no longer traveling but settling in at the church's cost; that marks him a "false prophet."
orig: οὐ μενεῖ δὲ εἰ μὴ ἡμέραν μίαν (ou menei de ei mē hēmeran mian)

a: If he asks for money, he is a false prophet
p: Jesus sent the Twelve out with no money (Matthew 10:9). The Didache makes asking for it the mark of a false prophet.
b: "Do not get gold or silver or copper to carry in your belts" is Jesus' rule (Matthew 10:9). Paul defends his right to support but chose to work so as to offer the good news free (1 Corinthians 9:14-18; Acts 20:33-35). 2 Peter 2:3 warns of false teachers who "Out of greed ... will use you to make money." In the Didache an apostle may take bread for the day's road, enough to reach his night's lodging, and nothing more.
orig: ἐὰν δὲ ἀργύριον αἰτῇ (ean de argyrion aitē)

a: speaking in the Spirit
p: En pneumati has no article: "in the Spirit" or "in a spirit," in a state of inspiration.
b: The phrase describes the prophet's speech while inspired. John says he "was in the Spirit" on the Lord's day (Revelation 1:10, the same Greek). Lake translates "in a spirit," which leaves room for a false spirit, as 11:8 then does ("not everyone who speaks in the Spirit is a prophet"). The Plain English Translation says "in the Spirit" in 11:7-12, as the prophet claims, and the Didache's tests decide whether the claim is true.
orig: λαλοῦντα ἐν πνεύματι (lalounta en pneumati)

a: this sin will not be forgiven
t: Testing a prophet and the sin against the Spirit
p: To test or judge a prophet speaking in the Spirit is called the sin that "will not be forgiven."
b: The words recall Matthew 12:31: "people will be forgiven for any sin and any blasphemy. But for blasphemy against the Spirit there will be no forgiveness." The Didache applies the saying to judging what a prophet says while inspired. That seems to clash with 1 John 4:1 ("Put the spirits to the test") and 1 Corinthians 14:29 ("let the others weigh what is said"), and with the Didache's own tests in 11:8-12. Kraft answers that where 1 John 4:1 "advocates a doctrinal test," the Didache "speaks of a testing of conduct": the tests look at the prophet's life ("the Lord's ways"), not at the words he speaks in the Spirit; once his way of life shows him true, his inspired words are not to be challenged.

a: the Lord's ways
p: A prophet is known by whether he has "the Lord's ways": a life like the Lord's.
b: Tropoi are habits, manners, a way of living. The test is Jesus' own: "You will know who they are from their fruit" (Matthew 7:16), said of false prophets who look like sheep but are wolves (Matthew 7:15). 11:9-12 then gives examples: a prophet who orders a meal for himself, does not practice what he teaches, or asks for money for himself is false.
orig: τοὺς τρόπους κυρίου (tous tropous kyriou)

a: orders a table set in the Spirit
p: A prophet who, "in the Spirit," calls for a meal must not eat from it himself.
b: Horizōn trapezan is "ordering (or appointing) a table." It may mean ordering a meal for the poor while speaking in the Spirit, or ordering the community's meal; if the prophet then eats it himself, he has used his gift to feed himself. The point is the same as with money in 11:6 and 11:12: a true prophet does not profit from his words.
orig: ὁρίζων τράπεζαν (horizōn trapezan)

a: acts out an earthly mystery of the church
p: Mystērion kosmikon ekklēsias: one of the most puzzling phrases in the book.
b: Kosmikos means "of the world," earthly or cosmic. A prophet "acts toward" (poiōn eis) such a mystery, but does not teach others to do the same, and is not to be judged, "for the prophets of old did the same." The likeliest sense is a symbolic act, as the old prophets did: Hosea's marriage to an unfaithful wife (Hosea 1:2-3), Isaiah walking stripped (Isaiah 20:2-3), Ezekiel's signs. Kraft asks whether Hosea 1-3 is in mind, "and the practice of 'spiritual marriage' in early Christianity": a prophet living with a woman as a sign of Christ and the church ("This mystery is a great one. And I am speaking about Christ and about the church," Ephesians 5:32), perhaps in celibate marriage. The Didache's caution, "not teaching others to do" it, shows it was strange enough to need a rule.
orig: ποιῶν εἰς μυστήριον κοσμικὸν ἐκκλησίας (poiōn eis mystērion kosmikon ekklēsias)

a: Give me silver
p: A prophet may ask for gifts for the needy, never for himself.
b: Argyria, "pieces of silver," is money: the singular argyrion is the word rendered "money" in 11:6. A prophet who says "in the Spirit" "Give me silver" is not to be heard; one who asks for others in need is not to be judged. Paul's collection for Jerusalem (2 Corinthians 8-9) and Agabus's prophecy of famine that led to help for Judea (Acts 11:27-30) are the kind of asking the Didache allows.
orig: δός μοι ἀργύρια (dos moi argyria)

a: Everyone who comes in the Lord's name
p: The words of the Hosanna psalm, "Blessed is the one who comes in the Lord's name," are used of every Christian traveler.
b: "Blessed is the one who comes in the Lord's name!" is Psalm 118:26, sung by the crowds in Matthew 21:9. Here "coming in the Lord's name" means arriving as a fellow Christian. Welcome comes first; testing follows. "Understanding of right and left" is an idiom for telling true from false, as Jonah 4:11 speaks of people "who do not know the difference between their right hand and their left."

a: so that no Christian will live idle among you
p: The name "Christian," which the New Testament uses only three times.
b: Christianos appears only three times in the New Testament (Acts 11:26; Acts 26:28; 1 Peter 4:16). Here it is used plainly, as a word the community uses of itself. The rule matches Paul's: "Whoever does not want to work should not eat either" (2 Thessalonians 3:10). The church is to find work for a newcomer without a trade, not keep him idle.
orig: Χριστιανός (Christianos)

a: Christ-peddler
p: Christemporos, a coined word: someone who makes a trade of Christ.
b: Christemporos joins "Christ" and emporos, "merchant, trader." Paul uses a similar picture: "For we are not like the many who peddle God's word" (2 Corinthians 2:17, with kapēleuō, to hawk goods). The word names someone who lives off the name of Christ instead of working. The warning "Be on your guard against" is the phrase Jesus uses of false prophets in Matthew 7:15.
orig: χριστέμπορος (christemporos)

a: has earned his food
p: The Didache gives Jesus' saying "A worker has earned his food" (Matthew 10:10) to prophets and teachers who settle.
b: Matthew 10:10 ends Jesus' instructions to the Twelve with "A worker has earned his food"; Luke and Paul have "wages" (Luke 10:7; 1 Timothy 5:18). The Didache's Greek has Matthew's word trophē, "food." A prophet or teacher who stays is no longer a traveler but a worker of the church, and the church feeds him.
orig: ἄξιός ἐστι τῆς τροφῆς αὐτοῦ (axios esti tēs trophēs autou)

a: for they are your high priests
p: The firstfruits Israel gave the priests (Numbers 18:12) go to the prophets, "your high priests."
b: The Law gave the priests the first of the grain, wine and oil and the first of the flocks (Numbers 18:12-13; Deuteronomy 18:4). The Didache keeps the custom for Gentile believers, with the prophets in the place of the priests, and calls them "your high priests." Kraft: "The ancient high priests are replaced by the prophets," and later forms of this tradition put "bishop" and other clergy here, or keep "priests." Whether that makes them priests in the later sense is part of the debate over priesthood (the site's cards at Hebrews 7 and 1 Peter 2). The list follows the farm year: winepress, threshing floor, cattle, sheep, then bread, wine, oil, silver and clothing (13:5-7).
orig: αὐτοὶ γάρ εἰσιν οἱ ἀρχιερεῖς ὑμῶν (autoi gar eisin hoi archiereis hymōn)

a: give them to the poor
p: If a church has no prophet, the firstfruits go to the poor: prophets were not in every church.
b: The verse shows that resident prophets were not found everywhere, and that the gifts were the poor's when no prophet claimed them. Deuteronomy sets aside the tithe of every third year for the Levite, the foreigner, the orphan and the widow (Deuteronomy 14:28-29). The Didache's "commandment" in 13:5 and 13:7 may point to such laws, or to a rule of Jesus known to the community.

a: On the Lord's day of the Lord
p: Kata kyriakēn de kyriou: the Greek doubles "of the Lord." Kraft takes it as the regular Sunday gathering.
b: Kyriakē is the adjective "the Lord's" (as in "the Lord's day," Revelation 1:10, and "the Lord's supper," 1 Corinthians 11:20), with "day" understood. The Didache adds "of the Lord" as well, so the phrase is literally "according to the Lord's (day) of the Lord." The Plain English Translation keeps the doubling. Christians gathered "on the first day of the week" to break bread (Acts 20:7; 1 Corinthians 16:2), the day of the resurrection. The Apostolic Constitutions makes it explicit: "On the day of the resurrection of the Lord, that is, the Lord's day, assemble yourselves together" (book 7, chapter 30). Kraft thinks it "probably" means "regular Sunday meetings," and notes that C. W. Dugmore argued only Easter is meant. Whether Sunday replaces the Sabbath is asked in the site's cards at Revelation 1 and Exodus 20.
orig: κατὰ κυριακὴν δὲ κυρίου (kata kyriakēn de kyriou)

a: break bread and give thanks
p: "Break bread and give thanks" on the Lord's day: Kraft notes it has "usually been interpreted as a Eucharistic service."
b: "To break bread" is the phrase of Acts for the church's meal (Acts 2:42, 46; 20:7). Here it comes with "give thanks" (eucharistēsate) and with "sacrifice," Kraft: the breaking of bread here "has usually been interpreted as a Eucharistic service (so Georg)," the Georgian version, "but the passage is by no means unambiguous and a regular community meal could be in view." Chapters 9-10 and 14 may describe two gatherings or the same one from two sides; the text does not say. How often the Supper should be held is asked in the site's card at Acts 20.

a: so that your sacrifice may be pure
p: The Didache calls the Sunday thanksgiving "your sacrifice" and quotes Malachi's "pure sacrifice."
b: Thysia is "sacrifice," the word for offerings on an altar. The Didache uses it three times in 14:1-3 and argues from it: the sacrifice must be pure, so confess first; it must not be made unclean, so be reconciled first; this is the pure sacrifice of Malachi. Kraft warns against jumping to the conclusion that it means the Eucharist, since "prayers and praise often were called 'sacrifices' in this period." What kind of sacrifice is meant is argued: the prayers and thanks of the church ("a sacrifice of praise," Hebrews 13:15), the believers offering themselves (Romans 12:1), or the bread and cup as an offering. Churches answer this differently; the site's cards at Malachi 1, Luke 22 and Hebrews 10 set out their views.
orig: ὅπως καθαρὰ ἡ θυσία ὑμῶν ᾖ (hopōs kathara hē thysia hymōn ē)

a: until they have made peace
p: Jesus' rule about the altar (Matthew 5:23-24) applied to the church's Sunday gathering.
b: "Leave the offering where it is, before the altar, and go. Make peace with your brother first, and then come and present your offering" (Matthew 5:24). The Didache uses the same verb, diallassō, and keeps anyone with an unsettled quarrel out of the gathering until the two have made peace, "so that your sacrifice is not made unclean." The rule ties worship to peace in the church, as 1 Corinthians 11:18-22 does.
orig: ἕως οὗ διαλλαγῶσιν (heōs hou diallagōsin)

a: In every place and time, present to me a pure sacrifice
p: The quotation joins Malachi 1:11 and 1:14, and follows the Greek "pure sacrifice" rather than the Hebrew "pure offering."
b: The site's Malachi 1:11, from the Hebrew, reads: "In every place incense is being burned and brought to my name, and a pure offering, for my name is great among the nations, says the LORD of Armies." The Hebrew minchah is a grain offering or gift; Swete's Septuagint has thysia kathara, "a pure sacrifice," and the Didache follows that Greek word, on which its argument turns. It also changes the prophet's statement into a command ("present to me"), adds "and time," and joins the end of Malachi 1:14: "For I am a great king, says the LORD of Armies, and my name is feared among the nations" (Malachi 1:14), where the Didache has "says the Lord" and "wonderful" (thaumaston; Swete's Greek has epiphanes, "manifest"). It introduces the words as "spoken by the Lord."
orig: θυσίαν καθαράν (thysian katharan)

a: overseers and deacons
