p: Episkopoi, the word behind "bishop," and diakonoi: chosen by the church, in the plural.
b: Episkopos (gloss: the word behind "bishop") means "overseer"; the site uses "overseer" everywhere, as in Philippians 1:1 ("with overseers and deacons") and 1 Timothy 3:1. The Didache has several overseers in one church, as Philippians and Acts 20:28 do, and names no single head over them. The verb cheirotoneō first meant to vote by raising hands, then to appoint; Acts 14:23 uses it when Paul and Barnabas "chose elders." Who chooses church leaders is the question of the site's card at Acts 14, and whether overseers are a separate order above elders is the question at 1 Timothy 3 and Philippians 1.
orig: ἐπισκόπους καὶ διακόνους (episkopous kai diakonous)

a: free from the love of money
p: The list echoes 1 Timothy 3: gentle, free from the love of money, truthful, tested.
b: "Free from the love of money" (aphilargyros) is the word of 1 Timothy 3:3, and "tested" (dedokimasmenous) matches "These also should be tested first" of deacons in 1 Timothy 3:10. "Gentle" is the word of 3:7 and of Matthew 5:5. The Didache's list is short, all about character, and says nothing of age or marriage.
orig: ἀφιλαργύρους (aphilargyrous)

a: the service of the prophets and teachers
p: Leitourgia: public worship service, the word behind "liturgy."
b: Leitourgia (gloss: public worship service, the word behind "liturgy") was a public duty done for a city; in the Greek Old Testament it is the priests' service in the sanctuary, and in Acts 13:2 the prophets and teachers at Antioch "were serving the Lord" (leitourgountōn). The Didache says overseers and deacons "perform for you the service of the prophets and teachers": they are taking over the work traveling and resident prophets did, which may be why it must add, "do not look down on them" (15:2).
orig: λειτουργοῦσι ... τὴν λειτουργίαν (leitourgousi ... tēn leitourgian)

a: Correct each other, not in anger, but in peace
p: The rule points to the good news, probably to Matthew 18:15-17, and to cutting off the unrepentant.
b: "If your brother sins against you, go and correct him, with just the two of you there" (Matthew 18:15). The Didache adds "not in anger, but in peace" (compare Galatians 6:1, "with a gentle spirit"). For the one who will not repent, no one is to talk with him until he does, as in Matthew 18:17 ("regard him as you regard the Gentile and the tax collector") and 2 Thessalonians 3:14. Lake's margin also points to Matthew 5:22-26 and 18:15-35.
orig: ἐλέγχετε δὲ ἀλλήλους (elenchete de allēlous)

a: Stay awake over your life
p: The last chapter opens with Jesus' sayings about watching: lamps, belts, readiness, the unknown hour.
b: "Have your robes tucked into your belts and your lamps lit" (Luke 12:35); "So stay awake, since you know neither the day nor the hour" (Matthew 25:13); "you also need to be ready" (Matthew 24:44). The Didache gathers these into one call. "Do not let your belts come loose" is literally "let your loins not be loosened," the picture of robes tied up for work or travel.
orig: γρηγορεῖτε (grēgoreite)

a: unless you are made perfect in the last season
t: The whole time of your faith
p: Barnabas 4:9 has the same warning in almost the same words.
b: Barnabas 4:9 warns that all the time of our faith will do us no good unless we stand firm now, in the lawless season, a verse Lake's margin cites; the Greek ho pas chronos tēs pisteōs is shared word for word. Both stress that faith must hold to the end, as Jesus says, "whoever holds out to the end, that person will be saved" (Matthew 24:13). "Come together often" is like Hebrews 10:25: "We must not walk out on our gatherings."
orig: ὁ πᾶς χρόνος τῆς πίστεως ὑμῶν (ho pas chronos tēs pisteōs hymōn)

a: The sheep will turn into wolves
p: Jesus warned of false prophets "dressed up as sheep" who are wolves (Matthew 7:15). Here sheep become wolves.
b: The chapter follows Jesus' sayings on the Mount of Olives (Matthew 24): "Many false prophets will rise up and lead many people astray. Lawlessness will multiply, and because of it the love of many will go cold" (Matthew 24:11-12). Paul warned the Ephesian elders that "vicious wolves will get in among you" and that men would rise "out of your own group" (Acts 20:29-30). In the Didache the danger is from inside: the church's own sheep turn into wolves, and "the corrupters" multiply (phthoreis, the word rendered "destroyers" in 5:2, where it goes with "what God has formed").

a: the world-deceiver
p: Kosmoplanēs, "deceiver of the world": the figure the New Testament calls the man of lawlessness or the antichrist.
b: The Didache's word is found nowhere in the New Testament, but the figure is there: "the lawless one" whose coming is with "signs and wonders that are a lie" (2 Thessalonians 2:9), the beast "given authority over every tribe, people, language, and nation" (Revelation 13:7), and "the deceiver and the antichrist" of 2 John 1:7. He appears "as a son of God": either claiming to be one, or like God's Son as a false copy. "Signs and wonders" is Matthew 24:24, and "never happened, ever" recalls Matthew 24:21: "Nothing like it has happened from the start of the world until now."
orig: ὁ κοσμοπλανής (ho kosmoplanēs)

a: saved by the curse itself
p: Hyp' autou tou katathematos: one of the hardest phrases in the book, read in several ways.
b: Katathema is "a thing accursed" or "a curse" (as in Revelation 22:3, "Nothing will be under a curse any longer"). Kraft gives the readings. (1) Christ the accursed one: this is the sense of Kraft's own translation, "by him who was accursed." He compares Galatians 3:13, where Christ bought us free from the curse, "having become a curse for us," and Barnabas 7:9. (2) The curse itself, or "that which is cursed" (the earth? Genesis 3:17). (3) From the curse: the Georgian version has "something like 'from this frightful curse'," that is, the fiery test; J.-P. Audet took it as "from the grave itself." The Plain English Translation keeps the bare words. "The human creation" (hē ktisis tōn anthrōpōn) is all of humankind, and "the fire of testing" is like "the fiery ordeal" of 1 Peter 4:12.
orig: ὑπ᾽ αὐτοῦ τοῦ καταθέματος (hyp' autou tou katathematos)

a: the sign of something spread out in the sky
p: Sēmeion ekpetaseōs: an opening of the sky, or the cross with its arms spread out?
b: Ekpetasis is a spreading or stretching out. Matthew speaks of "the sign of the Son of Man" that "will show itself in the sky" (Matthew 24:30) but does not say what it is. Two readings fit the word: (1) the cross, the outstretched arms of the crucified, seen in the sky as the Son of Man's sign; Kraft points to the Ethiopic Apocalypse of Peter and the Epistle of the Apostles, which have the cross going before the Lord as he comes; Isaiah 65:2 says "I have spread out my hands all day long"; (2) the sky opening, spread back like a curtain or a scroll (compare Revelation 6:14, "The sky pulled away like a scroll as it rolls up"), for the Lord to come through. The trumpet follows, as in Matthew 24:31 and 1 Thessalonians 4:16.
orig: σημεῖον ἐκπετάσεως ἐν οὐρανῷ (sēmeion ekpetaseōs en ouranō)
r: Matthew 24:30-31; 1 Thessalonians 4:16; 1 Corinthians 15:52; Revelation 6:14; Isaiah 65:2; Isaiah 34:4

a: But not of all the dead
t: "Not of all": a resurrection of the righteous
p: The third sign is a resurrection, but "not of all": only the saints rise when the Lord comes.
b: "Not of all" limits the resurrection at the Lord's coming to "the saints." Paul says "Those who are dead in Christ will rise first" (1 Thessalonians 4:16) and "then, at his coming, those who belong to Christ" (1 Corinthians 15:23). Revelation separates "the first resurrection" from the rest of the dead (Revelation 20:5-6). The Didache may hold that only the righteous rise at all, or that the wicked rise later; it does not say. The site's topic first-resurrection and the millennium card at Revelation 20 give the views.

a: The Lord will come, and all the saints with him.
p: The quotation is Zechariah 14:5 in its Greek form, with "my God" left out.
b: The site's Zechariah 14:5, from the Hebrew, ends "And the LORD my God will arrive, and all the holy ones will be with you." Swete's Septuagint has "and the Lord my God will come, and all the holy ones with him" (kai pantes hoi hagioi met' autou), and the Didache follows that Greek, without "my God," introducing it with "as it has been said." In Zechariah the holy ones are likely angels; the Didache takes them as the risen saints, the "not of all" who rise. 1 Thessalonians 3:13 speaks of "the coming of our Lord Jesus with all his holy ones" in the same way.
orig: Ἥξει ὁ κύριος καὶ πάντες οἱ ἅγιοι μετ᾽ αὐτοῦ (Hēxei ho kyrios kai pantes hoi hagioi met' autou)

a: coming on the clouds of the sky
p: The one complete Greek manuscript stops here and leaves the rest of the page blank. The Georgian version goes on.
b: The last words echo Daniel 7:13 and Jesus' sayings: "They will see the Son of Man coming on the clouds of the sky" (Matthew 24:30; Matthew 26:64). Kraft: the Greek manuscript "concludes here (with the remainder of the page left blank), but both Georg and ApCo lack the words 'of heaven' and continue with a reference to the final judgment." His translation follows the Georgian ending: "... with power and dominion to repay each man according to his work, with justice, before all men and angels. Amen." The Apostolic Constitutions goes on to the Lord's coming "with a great concussion above the clouds" and ends: "Then shall the wicked go away into everlasting punishment, but the righteous shall go into life eternal" (book 7, chapter 32, in the Ante-Nicene Fathers translation, echoing Matthew 25:46). Kraft also allows that the Didache may have ended where the Greek manuscript does.
orig: ἐπάνω τῶν νεφελῶν τοῦ οὐρανοῦ (epanō tōn nephelōn tou ouranou)
r: Matthew 24:30; Matthew 26:64; Daniel 7:13; Revelation 1:7; Matthew 16:27; Matthew 25:46
